title: Tikhonov-Stabilized Bézier Representation Forecasting for Training-free Diffusion Acceleration

paper.title: Tikhonov-Stabilized Bézier Representation Forecasting for Training-free Diffusion Acceleration
paper.abstract:
Abstract Diffusion models, particularly Diffusion Transformers, achieve strong image and video generation quality but remain expensive at inference time due to repeated denoiser evaluations. Feature caching offers a deployment-friendly acceleration strategy by reusing or predicting intermediate representations without retraining the generator or modifying the sampler. However, existing cache-then-forecast methods often rely on Taylor-style finite-difference extrapolation, which can become unstable over longer cache intervals, and typically predict local module outputs whose errors may accumulate through subsequent denoiser blocks. We propose BeziCast , a training-free diffusion acceleration framework that forecasts output-proximal denoising representations using low-order Bézier trajectories. BeziCast estimates Bézier control points via Tikhonov-stabilized fitting, providing a smooth, capacity-controlled temporal parameterization that avoids explicit high-order derivative estimation and decouples trajectory capacity from cache-query density. To moderate aggressive extrapolation, we further derive equivalent forecasting weights and introduce a convex-hull-inspired guardrail that detects high-risk predictions and softly pulls them toward a conservative simplex-projected estimate.
Extensive evaluations across advanced image and video diffusion models demonstrate the effectiveness of BeziCast. In particular, BeziCast accelerates FLUX.1 by up to 4.79 × 4.79\times and HunyuanVideo by up to 4.11 × 4.11\times , while preserving substantially better generation quality than competing acceleration baselines.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Diffusion models Ho et al. (2020) , especially large generative models based on Diffusion Transformer Peebles and Xie (2023) ; Esser et al. (2024) ; Zhu et al. (2026a) ; Kong et al. (2024) , have become a standard approach for high-fidelity image and video generation. Their sampling process, however, still requires repeated denoiser evaluations across many timesteps, and this inference cost remains a major obstacle to large-scale deployment. A central question in diffusion acceleration is how to approximate the original multi-step sampling process under a limited NFE budget Lu et al. (2022) ; Zhao et al. (2023) . Existing approaches can be broadly grouped into three directions. Solver-based methods improve the sampler through higher-order updates Lu et al. (2022) ; Lu et al. (2025) ; Zhao et al. (2023) , timestep schedules Karras et al. (2022) , and trajectory-aware error correction or time allocation Zhou et al. (2024b) ; Wang et al. (2025) ; Chen et al. (2024) ; Zhou et al. (2024a) ; Zhu et al. (2026b) ; Wang et al. (2024) ; Zhou et al. (2026) ; Min et al. (2026) . Distillation-based methods compress multi-step sampling into few-step or one-step generation through progressive distillation Salimans and Ho (2022) , consistency modeling Luo et al. (2023) , or distribution matching Yin et al. (2024b) . Feature caching methods instead keep the pretrained generator largely unchanged and reduce the cost of each denoiser evaluation by reusing or predicting internal representations Ma et al. (2024) ; Liu et al. (2025c) . Compared with the former two directions, feature caching is particularly deployment-friendly because it avoids retraining the full model and does not require redesigning the sampling dynamics. Early training-free feature caching methods mainly followed a cache-then-reuse paradigm, where intermediate features from nearby timesteps are directly reused to skip selected layers or modules Ma et al. (2024) ; Selvaraju et al. (2024) ; Liu et al. (2025e) ; Ma et al. (2025) . Recent methods move toward cache-then-forecast . TaylorSeer Liu et al. (2025c) predicts future features with finite differences and Taylor expansion, and Figure 1: Stable, Fast, and Accurate Diffusion Acceleration. Left : PC1 projections of output-proximal representation in denoising step. Right : Speedup and PSNR comparison, where N N is the cache interval. BeziCast achieves faster inference while better quality. SpeCa Liu et al. (2025d) adds a lightweight verifier to accept or reject predicted features. Spectrum Han et al. (2026) takes a global function-approximation view by fitting Chebyshev polynomial coefficients for final-layer denoiser features and deriving a horizon-independent error bound under its approximation setting. These methods show that denoiser representations have exploitable temporal regularity, but they also leave two design choices: which representation should be predicted, and which temporal basis should be used. The first design choice is the temporal basis . Taylor-style predictors are simple, but finite-difference derivative estimates and local power-basis extrapolation can amplify small cache perturbations at longer offsets or higher orders Liu et al. (2025c) ; Li et al. (2023) ; Feng et al. (2026) , as evidenced by the instability of the blue curve and its large deviation from the ground truth on the left of Fig. 1 . This sensitivity is consistent with the numerical behavior of monomial and Vandermonde-type systems Shen and Serkh (2025) , the non-monotone feature trajectories discussed by Feng et al. Feng et al. (2026) , and the large-horizon error growth observed by Han et al. Han et al. (2026) . At the same time, diffusion sampling trajectories often exhibit structured low-dimensional geometry Chen et al. (2025) . We therefore seek a compact temporal parameterization that avoids explicit high-order finite differences while remaining analytically evaluable at cache steps. The second design choice is the forecasting target . Existing caching methods often predict attention outputs, MLP outputs inside transformer blocks Selvaraju et al. (2024) ; Ma et al. (2025) ; Zhu et al. (2025) ; Liu et al. (2025d) . These local targets give fine-grained control, but their errors still pass through downstream denoiser blocks before reaching the final noise estimate and may accumulate across predicted modules. We instead predict an output-proximal denoising representation, which makes the path from representation error to denoising error shorter and more direct without assuming that this representation is intrinsically easier to forecast. Based on these observations, we propose BeziCast , a training-free Tikhonov-stabilized Bézier representation forecasting framework, achieving faster, more stable, and more accurate acceleration than competing methods , as shown on the right of Fig. 1 . BeziCast predicts an output-proximal denoising representation with a low-order Bernstein/Bézier trajectory whose control points are estimated by Tikhonov-stabilized fitting. The Bézier form provides analytic evaluation and a compact capacity-controlled function family Farouki and Rajan (1987) ; Wu et al. (2026) ; Patrikalakis et al. (2009) , while the Bernstein basis has classical stability properties on a fixed interval Farouki and Goodman (1996) , as shown by the orange curve on the left of Fig. 1 , which is closer to the ground truth than Taylor-based extrapolation. Because cache queries are often short-range extrapolations, BeziCast does not use the convex-hull property as a guarantee; instead, it uses equivalent weights to detect signed or non-affine extrapolation and pulls high-risk predictions toward a simplex-projected conservative estimate. The pretrained denoiser and sampler remain unchanged. Our contributions are as follows: (1) We formulate training-free cache-then-forecast acceleration as output-proximal representation forecasting, avoiding multiple local module targets. (2) We use a low-order Bernstein/Bézier trajectory with Tikhonov-stabilized control-point fitting, replacing finite-difference Taylor extrapolation, decoupling trajectory capacity from cache-query density, and expressing each prediction as a regularized linear combination of cached representations. (3) We introduce an equivalent-weight convex-hull guardrail that detects aggressive extrapolation through negative weight mass, deviation from unit sum, and the ℓ 1 \ell_{1} norm, then pulls high-risk predictions toward a simplex-projected conservative estimate.

sections.heading: 2 Related Work
sections.text: Diffusion acceleration methods mainly reduce either the number of denoising steps, the cost of each denoising step, or both. Sampler-based Acceleration. Sampler-based methods reduce the number of function evaluations by improving the reverse diffusion discretization. DDIM Song et al. (2020) enables deterministic non-Markovian sampling from DDPM Ho et al. (2020) models with fewer steps. DPM-Solver Lu et al. (2022) and DPM-Solver++ Lu et al. (2025) derive high-order ODE solvers for probability-flow sampling, UniPC Zhao et al. (2023) unifies predictor-corrector updates, and EDM Karras et al. (2022) improves noise parameterization, preconditioning, and sampling schedules. Recent trajectory-aware methods further exploit path regularity, error correction, or time allocation, including AMED-Solver Zhou et al. (2024b) , Trajectory Regularity Chen et al. (2024) , Simple and Fast Distillation Zhou et al. (2024a) , PAS Wang et al. (2025) , PFDiff Wang et al. (2024) , fast-sampling analysis Zhou et al. (2026) , and BézierFlow Min et al. (2026) . These methods mainly accelerate sampling by changing the solver, schedule, or trajectory correction strategy. Training-based Acceleration. Training-based methods compress a multi-step teacher into a faster generator through extra optimization. Progressive Distillation Salimans and Ho (2022) halves sampling steps iteratively; Consistency Models Song et al. (2023) and Latent Consistency Models Luo et al. (2023) enforce trajectory-consistent predictions for few-step generation; DMD Yin et al. (2024b) and DMD2 Yin et al. (2024a) match the teacher distribution rather than the full teacher trajectory; and InstaFlow Liu et al. (2023) uses rectified-flow-style training to straighten text-to-image generation paths. These approaches can be effective, but they usually require additional training, teacher models, or specialized objectives. Feature-caching-based Acceleration. Feature-caching methods Liu et al. (2025c) ; Yang et al. (2024) ; Selvaraju et al. (2024) ; Yang et al. (2025) reduce inference cost by exploiting temporal redundancy in denoiser activations while keeping the pretrained denoiser largely unchanged. Early cache-then-reuse methods directly reuse intermediate features or residuals: DeepCache Ma et al. (2024) reuses high-level U-Net features, FORA Selvaraju et al. (2024) extends fast-forward caching to diffusion transformers, ToCa Zou et al. (2024) introduces token-wise feature caching, and Reuse and Diffuse Gu et al. (2023) plus MagCache Ma et al. (2025) study feature or residual reuse for video diffusion. Recent cache-then-forecast methods model feature evolution instead of copying old features: TaylorSeer Liu et al. (2025c) uses finite differences and Taylor expansion, FreqCa Liu et al. (2025b) adds frequency-aware caching, Forecast-then-Calibrate Zheng et al. (2026) introduces feature calibration, HiCache Feng et al. (2026) replaces Taylor-style monomial forecasting with Hermite-polynomial-based prediction, and Spectrum Han et al. (2026) fits global spectral approximations. Adaptive variants such as TeaCache Liu et al. (2025a) , DiCache Bu et al. (2026) , SpeCa Liu et al. (2025d) , and token-level cache updates Zheng et al. (2025) further show that diffusion features exhibit strong temporal and structural redundancy. BeziCast follows the training-free cache-then-forecast line, but focuses on output-proximal representation forecasting with a Tikhonov-stabilized Bézier trajectory and an equivalent-weight guardrail for extrapolation risk.

sections.heading: 3 Method
sections.text: Figure 2: Overview of BeziCast. (a) A local cubic Bernstein/Bézier trajectory is fitted from cached full-step representations and evaluated at cache queries u s > 1 u_{s}>1 , providing a low-order alternative to Taylor-style extrapolation. (b) BeziCast detects risky extrapolation via equivalent history weights, constructs a simplex-projected prediction inside the cached-representation convex hull, and softly blends it with the raw forecast to obtain the guarded prediction. BeziCast is a training-free cache-then-forecast method for diffusion sampling. We recast feature prediction as output-proximal representation trajectory approximation: from a short history of denoising representations near the output, the method estimates a low-order Bézier trajectory and evaluates it at skipped cache steps. As shown in Fig. 2 , BeziCast runs the original denoiser at selected full steps, caches output-proximal representations, predicts them at cache steps with Tikhonov-stabilized Bernstein fitting, and applies the guardrail when needed. It does not train additional models, modify the sampler, or change the pretrained denoiser. This section first defines the cache-then-forecast setting, then gives the predictor and guardrail. The full inference algorithm is provided in Appendix A.4 .

sections.heading: Models and Tasks.
sections.text: For text-to-image generation, we evaluate BeziCast on FLUX.1-dev Esser et al. (2024) using a 50-step reference schedule and the 200-prompt DrawBench suite Saharia et al. (2022) , generating images at 1024 × 1024 1024\times 1024 . For text-to-video generation, we use HunyuanVideo Kong et al. (2024) and follow the official VBench Huang et al. (2024) prompt set and evaluation protocol.

sections.heading: Baselines and Metrics.
sections.text: We compare BeziCast with representative training-free acceleration methods, including κ \kappa -step sampling, cache-reuse methods FORA Selvaraju et al. (2024) , ToCa Zou et al. (2024) , and TeaCache Liu et al. (2025a) , as well as forecasting-based methods TaylorSeer Liu et al. (2025c) and HiCache Feng et al. (2026) . We use 𝒩 \mathcal{N} for the cache interval, n n for the number of Bézier control representations, and λ \lambda for Tikhonov regularization. We report sampling latency (per-image/video) and speedup relative to the original 50-step sampler, together with task-specific quality metrics: PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, ImageReward, and CLIP Score Hessel et al. (2021) for text-to-image generation; PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, and VBench Quality Score for text-to-video generation. Figure 4: Qualitative comparison on text-to-image generation using FLUX.1. BeziCast delivers the highest speedup while preserving prompt alignment, text readability, and visual fidelity.

sections.heading: 4.2 Main Comparisons.
sections.text: Figure 5: Qualitative comparison on text-to-video generation using HunyuanVideo. BeziCast closely follow the 50-step reference, whereas TaylorSeer is slower and introduces visible artifacts.

sections.heading: Text-to-Image Generation.
sections.text: The left part of Table 1 reports the quantitative results on FLUX.1-dev. BeziCast achieves a strong trade-off between acceleration and generation quality under both caching intervals. With 𝒩 = 4 \mathcal{N}=4 , BeziCast ( λ = 0.5 \lambda=0.5 ) uses 15 network evaluations, reaches a 3.47 × 3.47\times speedup, and obtains the best reference-based fidelity among accelerated methods. Compared with TaylorSeer and HiCache under similar budgets, BeziCast better preserves the 50-step reference, suggesting that Bézier trajectory forecasting provides a more accurate approximation than Taylor-style or Hermite-based extrapolation. Under the more aggressive setting with 𝒩 = 6 \mathcal{N}=6 , BeziCast uses 12 network evaluations, achieves a 4.79 × 4.79\times speedup, and maintains competitive quality. It outperforms direct reuse methods and forecasting baselines in reference alignment, achieving the best PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, and ImageReward score among all 𝒩 = 6 \mathcal{N}=6 methods. These results demonstrate the robustness of output-proximal Bézier forecasting for training-free text-to-image acceleration. Fig. 4 provides a qualitative comparison. BeziCast achieves the highest speedup while preserving prompt alignment, text legibility, and global visual fidelity comparable to the full FLUX.1 baseline.

sections.heading: Text-to-Video Generation.
sections.text: The right part of Table 1 reports the quantitative results on HunyuanVideo using VBench. BeziCast achieves strong text-to-video acceleration, reaching up to a 4.11 × 4.11\times wall-clock speedup while preserving high sample fidelity. With 𝒩 = 5 \mathcal{N}=5 , BeziCast ( n = 4 , λ = 0.5 n=4,\lambda=0.5 ) achieves a 3.60 × 3.60\times speedup and the best overall fidelity among accelerated methods. Compared with TaylorSeer and HiCache at similar speedups, BeziCast better matches the full-sampling reference, suggesting that Bézier-based forecasting more accurately approximates latent dynamics. Even under the more aggressive 𝒩 = 6 \mathcal{N}=6 setting, BeziCast maintains strong quality with a 4.11 × 4.11\times speedup, yielding a better efficiency–fidelity trade-off than competing baselines. Fig. 5 further shows that BeziCast more closely follows the 50-step reference and introduces fewer visible artifacts than TaylorSeer.

sections.heading: Perturbation Injection Diagnostic.
sections.text: We further apply the perturbation-injection diagnostic from Appendix A.2 to measure how errors at different forecasting targets affect the final denoising output . Following the local error-propagation analysis in Appendix A.2 , intermediate-target errors must traverse the remaining downstream blocks, while output-proximal errors only pass through the final output map. As shown in Fig. 6 (b), the final output-proximal representation achieves the highest robustness score among all tested targets, including double-stream block residuals and outputs at layers 6, 10, 14, and 18. Intermediate residuals are generally more robust than block outputs, and later layers are more robust than earlier ones, but all remain less robust than the output-proximal representation. This supports our target choice: BeziCast does not require the final hidden state to be easier to predict, but benefits from its shorter error-propagation path to the denoising output.

sections.heading: Equivalent-weight convex-hull guardrail
sections.text: Table 4: Effect of equivalent-weight convex-hull guardrails in the Flux.1. Variant PSNR ↑ \uparrow SSIM ↑ \uparrow LPIPS ↓ \downarrow CLIP ↑ \uparrow Rwd. ↑ \uparrow Lat. ↓ \downarrow None 20.993 0.750 0.115 27.192 1.028 10.109 PCA hull 20.930 0.750 0.115 27.214 1.031 10.150 Simplex 21.229 0.753 0.112 27.229 1.032 10.137 BeziCast uses equivalent history weights to diagnose extrapolation risk and constructs a conservative estimate by projecting high-risk weights onto the probability simplex. We compare three variants under the W = 6 W=6 FLUX schedule: no guardrail, a PCA convex-hull guardrail, and the simplex guardrail used in our main method. The PCA variant projects cached output-proximal representations into a low-dimensional PCA subspace, applies a convex-hull correction, and maps the estimate back to the original representation space. While lightweight, its behavior depends on the retained PCA subspace. Table 4 shows that the simplex guardrail provides the most stable reference-fidelity improvement with only minor latency overhead. In contrast, the PCA convex-hull guardrail slightly improves some semantic metrics but yields less consistent reference-fidelity gains. These results support using the simplex guardrail by default: rather than reinterpreting u > 1 u>1 Bézier extrapolation as standard convex-hull interpolation, it pulls high-risk forecasts toward a conservative estimate when the weights contain large negative entries or deviate from the affine constraint.

sections.heading: Number of control representations
sections.text: The number of control representations n n determines the degree and capacity of the Bézier trajectory, while the warm-up length W W controls how many initial solver steps are fully evaluated before forecasting begins. We ablate n ∈ { 4 , 5 , 6 } n\in\{4,5,6\} under W = 6 W=6 and W = 8 W=8 , with the Tikhonov coefficient fixed at λ = 5 × 10 − 1 \lambda=5\times 10^{-1} . As shown in Table 3 , increasing n n yields only marginal gains in reference fidelity, while the other quality metrics change little and latency may slightly increase. We therefore use n = 4 n=4 as the default setting, as it provides a stable cubic trajectory with competitive quality and the lowest or near-lowest latency.

sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: We presented BeziCast, a training-free diffusion acceleration framework that forecasts output-proximal denoising representations with low-order Bézier trajectories. With Bernstein fitting and a guardrail, BeziCast preserves the pretrained denoiser and sampler while improving the speed–quality trade-off on image and video generation. Experiments on FLUX.1, HunyuanVideo demonstrate substantial acceleration and stronger fidelity than cache-based baselines.

sections.heading: A.1.1 Design Motivation of Tikhonov-Stabilized Bernstein Basis
sections.text: The temporal basis determines how a cache-then-forecast method turns a short history of computed denoising representations into predictions at skipped timesteps [ 20 , 7 , 9 ] . Taylor-style predictors estimate local finite differences and extrapolate them in a Newton-form power basis [ 20 , 7 ] . This design is effective for short horizons, but it couples two sources of sensitivity: finite differences first form alternating high-order derivative estimates from nearby cached features, and extrapolation then multiplies these estimates by coefficients that grow with the forecast offset and expansion order. Proposition A.1 in Appendix A.1 makes this mechanism explicit: for an order- p p backward finite-difference predictor at future offset q q , bounded cache perturbations are amplified by a factor upper bounded by ∑ j = 0 p | ( q j ) | ​ 2 j \sum_{j=0}^{p}|\binom{q}{j}|2^{j} in Eq. ( 24 ), whose leading term grows as a degree- p p polynomial in q q . BeziCast replaces direct reuse and high-order finite-difference extrapolation with a regularized local trajectory fit. It estimates a low-order Bernstein/Bézier curve from recent output-proximal representations and evaluates the fitted curve at cache-step coordinates. A Bézier curve is defined by a small set of control points and Bernstein basis functions [ 6 ] ; once the control points are fixed, the curve can be evaluated analytically at any normalized time coordinate [ 30 ] . Thus, the number of control points sets trajectory capacity, while the cache schedule only determines how often the trajectory is queried. Cache forecasting differs from standard Bézier interpolation because future full-step representations are unavailable during online inference. At a cache step, the method observes only previously computed full steps, so the query is often a short-range extrapolation beyond the most recent full step, i.e., u > 1 u>1 . We therefore do not use the in-interval convex-hull property of Bézier curves as a direct correctness guarantee. Instead, we use the Bernstein/Bézier form as a smooth low-order trajectory family and explicitly control extrapolation through Tikhonov regularization, query-range clipping, and the equivalent-weight guardrail introduced in Section 3.3 . The Bernstein basis provides the geometric structure behind this design. On the standard interval u ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] u\in[0,1] , Bernstein basis functions are nonnegative and form a partition of unity, so the corresponding Bézier curve lies in the convex hull of its control points [ 30 ] . Farouki and Goodman further show that the Bernstein basis has optimal stability among nonnegative polynomial bases on a fixed interval [ 5 ] . Although cache prediction may query u > 1 u>1 , these properties remain useful as a diagnostic lens: after Tikhonov fitting, each prediction can be written as an equivalent linear combination of historical representations. If the equivalent weights become heavily signed or deviate from an affine combination, the forecast is relying on aggressive extrapolation rather than a conservative combination of observed features. This observation motivates both the regularized fitting below and the coefficient-space guardrail that follows [ 15 , 17 ] .

sections.text: We first ablate the representation used as the forecasting target. To isolate the target choice, we keep the pretrained FLUX denoiser, sampler, cache schedule, history length, Bernstein order, Tikhonov coefficient, and guardrail configuration fixed, and vary only the predicted representation. We compare three target types. Block-wise forecasting applies the same Bézier forecaster to local transformer-block outputs, resembling local-module feature caching where prediction errors are injected before subsequent blocks. Residual forecasting predicts the block residual/update representation, following the residual-style target used in prior caching methods. In our implementation, the residual is defined as the difference between the block output and the block input. Output-proximal forecasting predicts the final hidden representation z s z_{s} immediately before the output map 𝒪 θ \mathcal{O}_{\theta} , which is the default design of BeziCast. sections.heading: A.3 Warm-up and Fixed-period Full-step Schedule
sections.text: This subsection first defines the deterministic full-step schedule used by BeziCast, and then reports an ablation on the warm-up length. The schedule has two roles: the initial warm-up provides real output-proximal representations for the first local fit, and the later fixed-period full steps refresh the history used by cache-step forecasting.

sections.heading: A.3.1 Method Details
sections.text: BeziCast uses a warm-up plus fixed-period full-step schedule. The warm-up length W W is the number of initial solver steps evaluated by the full denoiser, and the fixed period R R specifies how often a full denoiser evaluation is inserted after warm-up. At full steps, BeziCast computes and caches the true output-proximal representation; at cache steps, it predicts the current representation from the most recent cached full-step representations. For a determined or over-determined control-point fit, the warm-up length should provide at least as many historical full-step representations as the number of Bernstein basis functions. Let n n denote the number of Bézier control representations. The default well-posed setting therefore uses W ≥ n . W\geq n. sections.text: Direct reuse is the zeroth-order case z ^ s = z i K \hat{z}_{s}=z_{i_{K}} . Taylor-style forecasting estimates local finite differences and extrapolates them in a power basis. Spectral predictors fit global polynomial bases over the denoising trajectory. BeziCast uses a local function-approximation form: it fits a short-history Bernstein/Bézier trajectory with Tikhonov regularization, evaluates it at cache steps, and writes the result as equivalent weights over historical output-proximal representations. The control-point number n n is chosen independently of the cache period.

sections.heading: Limitation.
sections.text: BeziCast is a training-free acceleration method and therefore preserves the pretrained denoiser and sampler, but its effectiveness depends on the temporal regularity of output-proximal denoising representations; when the denoising trajectory changes abruptly, aggressive cache intervals may still introduce prediction errors despite Tikhonov stabilization and the convex-hull guardrail. Its speed–quality trade-off is also sensitive to schedule and hyperparameters such as the warm-up length, cache period, Bézier control-point number, and regularization strength, which may require task- or model-specific tuning. In addition, our experiments mainly cover FLUX.1 for text-to-image generation and HunyuanVideo for text-to-video generation, so further validation on more architectures, samplers, resolutions, longer videos, and stronger downstream metrics is needed to fully establish generality. Finally, BeziCast assumes access to a suitable output-proximal representation and still executes the output map at cache steps, which may limit its applicability or acceleration benefit for architectures where such representations are inaccessible or the output head is non-negligible in cost.

Affiliation: School of Electronic and Computer Engineering, Peking University Abstract Diffusion models, particularly Diffusion Transformers, achieve strong image and video generation quality but remain expensive at inference time due to repeated denoiser evaluations. Feature caching offers a deployment-friendly acceleration strategy by reusing or predicting intermediate representations without retraining the generator or modifying the sampler. However, existing cache-then-forecast methods often rely on Taylor-style finite-difference extrapolation, which can become unstable over longer cache intervals, and typically predict local module outputs whose errors may accumulate through subsequent denoiser blocks. We propose BeziCast , a training-free diffusion acceleration framework that forecasts output-proximal denoising representations using low-order Bézier trajectories. BeziCast estimates Bézier control points via Tikhonov-stabilized fitting, providing a smooth, capacity-controlled temporal parameterization that avoids explicit high-order derivative estimation and decouples trajectory capacity from cache-query density. To moderate aggressive extrapolation, we further derive equivalent forecasting weights and introduce a convex-hull-inspired guardrail that detects high-risk predictions and softly pulls them toward a conservative simplex-projected estimate. Extensive evaluations across advanced image and video diffusion models demonstrate the effectiveness of BeziCast. In particular, BeziCast accelerates FLUX.1 by up to 4.79 × 4.79\times and HunyuanVideo by up to 4.11 × 4.11\times , while preserving substantially better generation quality than competing acceleration baselines. 1 Introduction Diffusion models Ho et al. (2020) , especially large generative models based on Diffusion Transformer Peebles and Xie (2023) ; Esser et al. (2024) ; Zhu et al. (2026a) ; Kong et al. (2024) , have become a standard approach for high-fidelity image and video generation. Their sampling process, however, still requires repeated denoiser evaluations across many timesteps, and this inference cost remains a major obstacle to large-scale deployment. A central question in diffusion acceleration is how to approximate the original multi-step sampling process under a limited NFE budget Lu et al. (2022) ; Zhao et al. (2023) . Existing approaches can be broadly grouped into three directions. Solver-based methods improve the sampler through higher-order updates Lu et al. (2022) ; Lu et al. (2025) ; Zhao et al. (2023) , timestep schedules Karras et al. (2022) , and trajectory-aware error correction or time allocation Zhou et al. (2024b) ; Wang et al. (2025) ; Chen et al. (2024) ; Zhou et al. (2024a) ; Zhu et al. (2026b) ; Wang et al. (2024) ; Zhou et al. (2026) ; Min et al. (2026) . Distillation-based methods compress multi-step sampling into few-step or one-step generation through progressive distillation Salimans and Ho (2022) , consistency modeling Luo et al. (2023) , or distribution matching Yin et al. (2024b) . Feature caching methods instead keep the pretrained generator largely unchanged and reduce the cost of each denoiser evaluation by reusing or predicting internal representations Ma et al. (2024) ; Liu et al. (2025c) . Compared with the former two directions, feature caching is particularly deployment-friendly because it avoids retraining the full model and does not require redesigning the sampling dynamics. Early training-free feature caching methods mainly followed a cache-then-reuse paradigm, where intermediate features from nearby timesteps are directly reused to skip selected layers or modules Ma et al. (2024) ; Selvaraju et al. (2024) ; Liu et al. (2025e) ; Ma et al. (2025) . Recent methods move toward cache-then-forecast . TaylorSeer Liu et al. (2025c) predicts future features with finite differences and Taylor expansion, and Figure 1: Stable, Fast, and Accurate Diffusion Acceleration. Left : PC1 projections of output-proximal representation in denoising step. Right : Speedup and PSNR comparison, where N N is the cache interval. BeziCast achieves faster inference while better quality. SpeCa Liu et al. (2025d) adds a lightweight verifier to accept or reject predicted features. Spectrum Han et al. (2026) takes a global function-approximation view by fitting Chebyshev polynomial coefficients for final-layer denoiser features and deriving a horizon-independent error bound under its approximation setting. These methods show that denoiser representations have exploitable temporal regularity, but they also leave two design choices: which representation should be predicted, and which temporal basis should be used. The first design choice is the temporal basis . Taylor-style predictors are simple, but finite-difference derivative estimates and local power-basis extrapolation can amplify small cache perturbations at longer offsets or higher orders Liu et al. (2025c) ; Li et al. (2023) ; Feng et al. (2026) , as evidenced by the instability of the blue curve and its large deviation from the ground truth on the left of Fig. 1 . This sensitivity is consistent with the numerical behavior of monomial and Vandermonde-type systems Shen and Serkh (2025) , the non-monotone feature trajectories discussed by Feng et al. Feng et al. (2026) , and the large-horizon error growth observed by Han et al. Han et al. (2026) . At the same time, diffusion sampling trajectories often exhibit structured low-dimensional geometry Chen et al. (2025) . We therefore seek a compact temporal parameterization that avoids explicit high-order finite differences while remaining analytically evaluable at cache steps. The second design choice is the forecasting target . Existing caching methods often predict attention outputs, MLP outputs inside transformer blocks Selvaraju et al. (2024) ; Ma et al. (2025) ; Zhu et al. (2025) ; Liu et al. (2025d) . These local targets give fine-grained control, but their errors still pass through downstream denoiser blocks before reaching the final noise estimate and may accumulate across predicted modules. We instead predict an output-proximal denoising representation, which makes the path from representation error to denoising error shorter and more direct without assuming that this representation is intrinsically easier to forecast. Based on these observations, we propose BeziCast , a training-free Tikhonov-stabilized Bézier representation forecasting framework, achieving faster, more stable, and more accurate acceleration than competing methods , as shown on the right of Fig. 1 . BeziCast predicts an output-proximal denoising representation with a low-order Bernstein/Bézier trajectory whose control points are estimated by Tikhonov-stabilized fitting. The Bézier form provides analytic evaluation and a compact capacity-controlled function family Farouki and Rajan (1987) ; Wu et al. (2026) ; Patrikalakis et al. (2009) , while the Bernstein basis has classical stability properties on a fixed interval Farouki and Goodman (1996) , as shown by the orange curve on the left of Fig. 1 , which is closer to the ground truth than Taylor-based extrapolation. Because cache queries are often short-range extrapolations, BeziCast does not use the convex-hull property as a guarantee; instead, it uses equivalent weights to detect signed or non-affine extrapolation and pulls high-risk predictions toward a simplex-projected conservative estimate. The pretrained denoiser and sampler remain unchanged. Our contributions are as follows: (1) We formulate training-free cache-then-forecast acceleration as output-proximal representation forecasting, avoiding multiple local module targets. (2) We use a low-order Bernstein/Bézier trajectory with Tikhonov-stabilized control-point fitting, replacing finite-difference Taylor extrapolation, decoupling trajectory capacity from cache-query density, and expressing each prediction as a regularized linear combination of cached representations. (3) We introduce an equivalent-weight convex-hull guardrail that detects aggressive extrapolation through negative weight mass, deviation from unit sum, and the ℓ 1 \ell_{1} norm, then pulls high-risk predictions toward a simplex-projected conservative estimate. 2 Related Work Diffusion acceleration methods mainly reduce either the number of denoising steps, the cost of each denoising step, or both. Sampler-based Acceleration. Sampler-based methods reduce the number of function evaluations by improving the reverse diffusion discretization. DDIM Song et al. (2020) enables deterministic non-Markovian sampling from DDPM Ho et al. (2020) models with fewer steps. DPM-Solver Lu et al. (2022) and DPM-Solver++ Lu et al. (2025) derive high-order ODE solvers for probability-flow sampling, UniPC Zhao et al. (2023) unifies predictor-corrector updates, and EDM Karras et al. (2022) improves noise parameterization, preconditioning, and sampling schedules. Recent trajectory-aware methods further exploit path regularity, error correction, or time allocation, including AMED-Solver Zhou et al. (2024b) , Trajectory Regularity Chen et al. (2024) , Simple and Fast Distillation Zhou et al. (2024a) , PAS Wang et al. (2025) , PFDiff Wang et al. (2024) , fast-sampling analysis Zhou et al. (2026) , and BézierFlow Min et al. (2026) . These methods mainly accelerate sampling by changing the solver, schedule, or trajectory correction strategy. Training-based Acceleration. Training-based methods compress a multi-step teacher into a faster generator through extra optimization. Progressive Distillation Salimans and Ho (2022) halves sampling steps iteratively; Consistency Models Song et al. (2023) and Latent Consistency Models Luo et al. (2023) enforce trajectory-consistent predictions for few-step generation; DMD Yin et al. (2024b) and DMD2 Yin et al. (2024a) match the teacher distribution rather than the full teacher trajectory; and InstaFlow Liu et al. (2023) uses rectified-flow-style training to straighten text-to-image generation paths. These approaches can be effective, but they usually require additional training, teacher models, or specialized objectives. Feature-caching-based Acceleration. Feature-caching methods Liu et al. (2025c) ; Yang et al. (2024) ; Selvaraju et al. (2024) ; Yang et al. (2025) reduce inference cost by exploiting temporal redundancy in denoiser activations while keeping the pretrained denoiser largely unchanged. Early cache-then-reuse methods directly reuse intermediate features or residuals: DeepCache Ma et al. (2024) reuses high-level U-Net features, FORA Selvaraju et al. (2024) extends fast-forward caching to diffusion transformers, ToCa Zou et al. (2024) introduces token-wise feature caching, and Reuse and Diffuse Gu et al. (2023) plus MagCache Ma et al. (2025) study feature or residual reuse for video diffusion. Recent cache-then-forecast methods model feature evolution instead of copying old features: TaylorSeer Liu et al. (2025c) uses finite differences and Taylor expansion, FreqCa Liu et al. (2025b) adds frequency-aware caching, Forecast-then-Calibrate Zheng et al. (2026) introduces feature calibration, HiCache Feng et al. (2026) replaces Taylor-style monomial forecasting with Hermite-polynomial-based prediction, and Spectrum Han et al. (2026) fits global spectral approximations. Adaptive variants such as TeaCache Liu et al. (2025a) , DiCache Bu et al. (2026) , SpeCa Liu et al. (2025d) , and token-level cache updates Zheng et al. (2025) further show that diffusion features exhibit strong temporal and structural redundancy. BeziCast follows the training-free cache-then-forecast line, but focuses on output-proximal representation forecasting with a Tikhonov-stabilized Bézier trajectory and an equivalent-weight guardrail for extrapolation risk. 3 Method Figure 2: Overview of BeziCast. (a) A local cubic Bernstein/Bézier trajectory is fitted from cached full-step representations and evaluated at cache queries u s > 1 u_{s}>1 , providing a low-order alternative to Taylor-style extrapolation. (b) BeziCast detects risky extrapolation via equivalent history weights, constructs a simplex-projected prediction inside the cached-representation convex hull, and softly blends it with the raw forecast to obtain the guarded prediction. BeziCast is a training-free cache-then-forecast method for diffusion sampling. We recast feature prediction as output-proximal representation trajectory approximation: from a short history of denoising representations near the output, the method estimates a low-order Bézier trajectory and evaluates it at skipped cache steps. As shown in Fig. 2 , BeziCast runs the original denoiser at selected full steps, caches output-proximal representations, predicts them at cache steps with Tikhonov-stabilized Bernstein fitting, and applies the guardrail when needed. It does not train additional models, modify the sampler, or change the pretrained denoiser. This section first defines the cache-then-forecast setting, then gives the predictor and guardrail. Taylor-style predictors estimate finite differences and extrapolate them in a Newton-form power basis. BeziCast uses a low-order Bernstein/Bézier trajectory with Tikhonov-stabilized fitting. Since future full-step representations are unavailable during online inference, cache-step prediction is typically performed by extrapolating beyond the recent history window.
